The primary rainbow we see is the result of light undergoing one internal reflection. This is why it appears as a single arc with the colors in a specific order: red on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge.

In the case of the Müller-Lyer illusion, the arrowheads can create the perception of depth, leading the brain to misjudge the length of the lines. This misjudgment is a result of the brain's attempt to maintain size constancy, which is the ability to perceive the size of objects as constant despite changes in distance or perspective. This theory can help explain why certain visual illusions occur and how the brain processes spatial information.
